comparison: Both strongly support the library construction methodology (C6, C22-C23, C26-C32, C89-C90). OpenEval emphasizes experimental data and methodological detail, while peer reviewers describe the platform as 'compelling' and 'detailed and convincing.' Peer review also includes C70 (diversity comparison) which OpenEval addresses separately in R10.

Both support the antigen production system (C34-C40). OpenEval focuses on vector design rationale and reproducibility, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the overall 'convincing' screening methodology. Peer review R2 also encompasses screening results (C41-C50) which OpenEval addresses separately in R3.

Both support the screening results and progressive enrichment (C41-C50). OpenEval provides detailed analysis of ELISA validation and notes the modest 62.5% success rate. Peer reviewers describe the data as 'convincing' and accept the screening methodology as valid.

Both support the transparent reporting of negative results (C51-C52, C77). OpenEval commends the honest acknowledgment of limitations, while peer reviewers implicitly accept these failures and focus on future protocol improvements to increase success rates.

Both support the computational structural predictions (C53-C56). OpenEval notes these are predictions without experimental validation, limiting confidence in specific residue interactions. Peer reviewers do not challenge the modeling approach and implicitly accept it as part of the 'convincing' overall validation.

Both support the cell surface binding validation (C57-C59). OpenEval highlights appropriate negative controls and notes one antigen (Amn) failed to display. Peer reviewers find data 'convincing' but note a weakness that many nanobodies fail to recognize membrane-tethered antigens.

Both strongly support the immunostaining application (C60, C62-C65). OpenEval emphasizes consistency with RNA-seq data and RNAi validation as strong evidence for specificity. Peer reviewers describe the immunostaining and immunoblotting data as 'convincing.'

Both support the immunoblotting application (C66-C67). OpenEval highlights genetic controls validating specificity and demonstrating nanobody versatility. Peer reviewers accept this as part of the overall 'convincing' application validation.

Both support the computational structural predictions for Mip-NbMip-4G complex (C68-C69). OpenEval notes these remain computational models without experimental structural validation. Peer reviewers do not raise concerns about the modeling approach.

Both support the phage vs. yeast platform comparison (C70-C73). OpenEval notes the diversity claim is data-supported but the affinity advantage remains speculative. Peer reviewers affirm this as an 'alternative platform' providing 'an excellent resource' while acknowledging room for improvement.

Both rate as UNCERTAIN the explanation for nanobodies failing in non-ELISA assays (C79). OpenEval notes the low affinity explanation is speculative without validation. Peer reviewers explicitly identify this as a weakness, stating 'this hypothesis has not been tested in the manuscript.'

OpenEval rates proposed improvements (C78, C80) as UNCERTAIN due to lack of experimental validation, while peer reviewers SUPPORT these suggestions. Peer reviewers view these as reasonable future directions that would 'greatly increase a successful rate,' aligning with the authors' proposals.

Both strongly support the open availability commitment (C9, C75). OpenEval notes the commitment is explicit though distribution mechanisms are not detailed. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm this as providing 'an excellent resource to the wider scientific community.'
